content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"Righteousness centrally means rightness according to God, encompassing both right standing before God and conformity to his will in upright conduct; traditions differ over whether saving righteousness is chiefly imputed, infused, covenantal, or enacted.","book_summary":"Righteousness is specifically the doing of God’s commandments—the law enacted in righteous deeds and symbolically worn as a garment—not merely general goodness or a forensic verdict received apart from conduct.","consensus_core_identification":"Rightness before God, expressed as a granted status and/or conformity to God’s moral will.","book_core_identification":"Actual obedience to God’s commandments and the resulting righteous acts.","core_relation":"BOOK_NARROWS","extension_relation":"BOOK_SUBSET","boundary_disagreement":"The book restricts righteousness to enacted commandment-keeping. It excludes vague moral goodness and, most materially, cases in which a person is called righteous solely by an imputed or forensic verdict without corresponding obedience. The consensus admits ethical obedience as a genuine sense but also includes status-based and other relational uses.","material_contradiction":"The book contradicts the dominant forensic view only where that view identifies righteousness as a received verdict independent of enacted obedience. It does not replace the consensus’s broader category of rightness according to God, because ethical obedience is already a recognized common component and alternative within that category.","rationale":"This is not novel: all three consensus responses explicitly recognize ethical or behavioral righteousness, and the cited texts are standard evidence for it. Nor is it a full core replacement, because both readings concern conformity to God’s standard. The book materially narrows the term’s extension by making commandment-doing constitutive and rejecting verdict-only cases, so REFINED is more appropriate than MATCH or DIVERGENT.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"Deuteronomy 6:25, Psalm 119:172, and 1 John 3:7 strongly establish that Scripture can call commandment-keeping and righteous action ‘righteousness,’ but they do not by themselves prove that this is the term’s exclusive meaning or rule out forensic, gifted, covenantal, or divine-righteousness uses elsewhere. The garment identification is also not directly demonstrated by the printed excerpts.","confidence":"high"}
